skill: Distinguishing the Performance Measurement Baseline (BAC) from unallocated Management Reserve when determining BAC for EVM purposes
scenario: A transmission line project's total control budget is $32,000,000. Of this, $30,000,000 is distributed across specific work packages and control accounts in the time-phased Performance Measurement Baseline (PMB), and the remaining $2,000,000 is held as Management Reserve, an amount senior management retains for unforeseen risks not yet allocated to any specific control account or work package.
question: What is the correct BAC to use for EVM calculations (CPI, SPI, EAC) on this project: $30,000,000 or $32,000,000? Explain why.
explanation: BAC for EVM purposes is $30,000,000, the Performance Measurement Baseline, since this is the total of the time-phased budget actually distributed to work packages and control accounts, against which Planned Value, Earned Value and all EVM indices are calculated. The $2,000,000 Management Reserve is deliberately excluded from BAC because it has not been allocated to any specific scope of work; it is held by management to be released into the PMB (increasing BAC) only if and when it is formally allocated to address a specific, realized risk or scope item. Until released, it is not part of the performance measurement system and should not be included in EVM calculations.
reasoning: This reflects the standard EVMS distinction between the Performance Measurement Baseline (the sum of all control account budgets, used for EV/PV/AC/BAC calculations) and Management Reserve (an unallocated contingency held above the PMB for management control, not yet tied to specific scope). Including Management Reserve in BAC would distort every EVM index, since PV and EV are built from control-account-level, time-phased budgets that Management Reserve, by definition, does not yet have.
commonMistakes: Including the full $32,000,000 total control budget as BAC, conflating total project budget with the Performance Measurement Baseline.
Not understanding that Management Reserve only becomes part of BAC once formally allocated to a control account.
Confusing Management Reserve with contingency held within individual control accounts (which, if allocated, is part of the PMB and would be included in BAC).
redFlags: Cannot distinguish Management Reserve from the Performance Measurement Baseline when asked what BAC should be.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If $500,000 of the Management Reserve is later formally released to the substation civil works control account to cover a confirmed ground condition risk, what happens to BAC?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding that BAC increases only when Management Reserve is formally allocated into the PMB, not automatically.

skill: Investigating an unexplained large favorable swing in the reported EAC before accepting it in the monthly report
scenario: A seaport container terminal package has BAC = $45,000,000. Last month's report showed EAC = $52,000,000. This month's report, with no specific corrective action, schedule recovery, descoped work, or root-cause explanation noted, shows EAC = $46,500,000, a favorable swing of $5,500,000 in a single reporting period.
question: Before accepting this month's improved EAC figure into the report, what would you check first?
expectedAnswer: Check whether the calculation methodology changed between the two periods, for example a switch between a bottom-up ETC and a CPI-based formula, or a change in which activities' costs are included, since a methodology change can produce a large swing that has nothing to do with genuine performance improvement. Check whether any large actual-cost correction occurred, such as a duplicate invoice being removed, a supplier credit being applied, or a batch of previously over-accrued cost being reversed, any of which would move AC (and therefore CPI-based EAC) sharply without reflecting a real trend change. Check whether the rules of credit or percent-complete basis changed, which would move EV. Check whether any scope was formally descoped (which should also reduce BAC, not just EAC) versus simply dropped from the forecast without a documented basis.
strongAnswer: Adds that the most efficient way to investigate is to decompose the swing into its components: how much of the $5,500,000 change is due to a change in AC (data correction), how much is due to a change in EV (progress/rules-of-credit change), and how much is due to a change in the ETC methodology or assumptions itself, since each of these has a different, specific verification path.
expertAnswer: Recommends that any EAC swing beyond an agreed materiality threshold (for example, more than 5-10% of BAC in a single period) should trigger a mandatory documented explanation before it is allowed into the report, not be accepted on the strength of the number alone, since large unexplained favorable swings are one of the most common ways an inaccurate or manipulated forecast slips past review, and once accepted without scrutiny, the credibility of the entire reporting process is at risk if the swing later proves to be a data error or an overly optimistic assumption.
explanation: A large, unexplained favorable EAC swing should never be accepted into a report without first decomposing it into its AC, EV, and methodology/assumption components, since each has a different, specific and verifiable cause, and one of the most common explanations for such swings is a data correction, methodology change, or optimistic reassumption rather than genuine performance improvement.
reasoning: EAC is a composite figure built from AC (an actual), EV (a measured quantity), and either an index or a bottom-up ETC (a judgment). A large swing in the composite number without a stated cause could originate from any of these three sources, and each source implies a very different level of confidence in the new figure: a genuine AC data correction is a one-time, defensible adjustment, while a quiet ETC assumption change without a stated corrective action is a red flag for forecast manipulation or unfounded optimism.
commonMistakes: Accepting a favorable EAC swing into the report simply because it is good news, without asking what changed.
Assuming a large favorable swing must reflect a genuine turnaround without verifying it against AC/EV component changes.
Not distinguishing a legitimate data correction from an unexplained assumption change.
redFlags: Would publish the improved EAC without decomposing what specifically changed since last month.
Cannot name concrete component-level checks (AC correction, EV/rules-of-credit change, ETC methodology change) when asked what to verify first.
p6Checks: Compare this month's AC to last month's AC plus this period's incurred cost to identify any retroactive adjustment.
Compare the ETC methodology and key assumptions documented in both months' reports.
Check whether any formal variation/descope was processed that would also require a BAC change, not just an EAC change.

skill: Explaining why SPI becomes unreliable late in a project and how Earned Schedule (ES) provides a more accurate, time-based alternative
scenario: A petrochemical EPC project is 92% complete by Earned Value (EV = 92% of BAC), giving SPI = EV/PV = 0.98, which the project team is reporting as 'essentially on schedule.' An independent Earned Schedule analysis, using the actual time elapsed against the time at which each increment of EV was planned to be earned, calculates that the project's Earned Schedule is 45 calendar days behind Actual Time, meaning the project is genuinely running about 45 days late relative to its baseline schedule, a materially different conclusion than 'essentially on schedule.'
question: Why can SPI show a near-1.0, apparently healthy value at 92% completion even though the project is genuinely 45 days behind schedule? What is Earned Schedule measuring differently, and which figure should be trusted?
explanation: SPI, defined as EV/PV, is denominated in dollars (or budget units), not time, and mathematically must converge toward 1.0 as a project approaches 100% completion, since EV cannot exceed BAC and PV also approaches BAC as the baseline nears its end: the 'gap' between EV and PV that SPI measures has a shrinking ceiling regardless of how many actual calendar days behind the project is running. This is a well-documented mathematical limitation of cost-based SPI, not a sign of genuine schedule recovery late in a project. Earned Schedule instead identifies, on the baseline PV curve, the time at which the current EV value would have been planned to be earned, and compares that to Actual Time elapsed; the resulting time-based gap (45 days behind, in this case) does not have the same end-of-project convergence-to-1.0 problem and gives a genuine, undistorted read of schedule health even very close to completion.
reasoning: This tests understanding of a known, real limitation of cost-based SPI that a senior/lead-level controls professional should be aware of: because BAC bounds both EV and PV, SPI necessarily trends toward 1.0 as a project nears completion, which can mask genuine, persistent schedule delay right when it matters most (near the end, close to a critical milestone or handover date). Earned Schedule, an extension to classical EVM, restates schedule performance in true time units specifically to correct this late-project distortion, and its output (Earned Schedule versus Actual Time, or the derived SPI(t) index) should be trusted over classical SPI whenever a project is more than roughly 70-80% complete.
commonMistakes: Reporting SPI near 1.0 late in a project as proof schedule performance has genuinely recovered, without checking Earned Schedule or the CPM forecast.
Not knowing that SPI is mathematically bounded to converge toward 1.0 as EV approaches BAC, regardless of true schedule health.
Dismissing Earned Schedule as an unnecessary complication rather than recognizing it addresses a specific, well-known SPI limitation.
redFlags: Reports 'essentially on schedule' based on late-project SPI without cross-checking against a time-based method or the CPM forecast finish date.
Cannot explain why SPI mathematically converges toward 1.0 near project completion.
p6Checks: Cross-check the CPM-calculated forecast finish date directly against the baseline finish date rather than relying on SPI alone this late in the project.
If Earned Schedule is being calculated, verify it is derived correctly from the baseline PV curve (the time at which current EV would have been planned) rather than approximated.

skill: Recalculating a plausible ETC from CPI and identifying an implausibly low reported ETC as a data-quality error
scenario: An airport baggage handling system package has BAC = $7,500,000. At the data date, EV = $5,000,000 (67% earned) and AC = $6,800,000. This month's cost report, submitted by a junior team member, shows a reported EAC of $6,900,000, implying an ETC (EAC - AC) of only $100,000 for the remaining 33% of scope.
question: Calculate CPI, then calculate the ETC that the typical-variance formula (BAC/CPI) would actually imply for the remaining work. Explain why the reported $100,000 ETC is implausible.
explanation: CPI = EV/AC = 5,000,000 / 6,800,000 = 0.735, an unfavorable trend on the 67% completed so far. The typical-variance EAC = BAC/CPI = 7,500,000 / 0.735 = $10,200,000, giving ETC = EAC - AC = 10,200,000 - 6,800,000 = $3,400,000. The reported $100,000 ETC is implausible on its face: it would require the remaining 33% of scope, roughly $2,500,000 of budgeted work (BAC - EV), to be completed for essentially nothing, on a package that has so far cost 36% more than budgeted for the value earned. There is no stated reason (design simplification, resolved constraint, new crew) for such a dramatic and immediate reversal in cost performance, so the reported figure is almost certainly a data or calculation error, not a genuine forecast.
reasoning: A basic but essential sanity check on any reported ETC is comparing it against what the remaining budgeted work (BAC - EV) would cost even at the currently demonstrated CPI, let alone at a worse or better rate. An ETC far below what the remaining budgeted work would cost even at CPI = 1.0 (here, remaining budgeted work alone is $2,500,000, already 25 times the reported $100,000 ETC) should be treated as an obvious red flag before it is accepted into any report.
commonMistakes: Accepting a reported ETC without checking it against the remaining budgeted work (BAC - EV) as a baseline sanity check.
Computing CPI as AC/EV instead of EV/AC.
Not questioning why a package with unfavorable CPI to date would suddenly need almost no further cost to complete.
redFlags: Would publish or accept an ETC without checking it against a simple order-of-magnitude sanity check.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What is the simplest, fastest sanity check you would teach a junior team member to catch this kind of error before it reaches a report?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests ability to translate a technical check into a practical, teachable habit.

skill: Aggregating PV, EV and AC across multiple buildings into a portfolio-level CPI and SPI, and flagging an anomalous cost-without-progress data point
scenario: A university campus programme has five buildings under construction at the data date: Building 1 (BAC $6,000,000, PV $6,000,000, EV $6,000,000, AC $6,300,000, complete); Building 2 (BAC $9,000,000, PV $7,200,000, EV $6,750,000, AC $7,000,000); Building 3 (BAC $4,500,000, PV $2,000,000, EV $1,800,000, AC $1,950,000); Building 4 (BAC $12,000,000, PV $3,000,000, EV $2,400,000, AC $2,900,000); Building 5 (BAC $3,500,000, PV $0, EV $0, AC $80,000, not yet due to start per the baseline).
question: Calculate the programme-wide BAC, PV, EV, AC, CPI and SPI. Separately, what is unusual about Building 5's figures, and what would you check?
correctAnswer: Programme BAC = $35,000,000; PV = $18,200,000; EV = $16,950,000; AC = $18,230,000; CPI = 0.930 (16,950,000/18,230,000); SPI = 0.931 (16,950,000/18,200,000). Building 5 has AC = $80,000 despite PV = EV = $0, meaning cost has been incurred on work not yet due to start per the baseline, which needs investigation.
explanation: Programme BAC = 6,000,000+9,000,000+4,500,000+12,000,000+3,500,000 = $35,000,000. PV = 6,000,000+7,200,000+2,000,000+3,000,000+0 = $18,200,000. EV = 6,000,000+6,750,000+1,800,000+2,400,000+0 = $16,950,000. AC = 6,300,000+7,000,000+1,950,000+2,900,000+80,000 = $18,230,000. CPI = EV/AC = 16,950,000/18,230,000 = 0.930. SPI = EV/PV = 16,950,000/18,200,000 = 0.931. Building 5's $80,000 of actual cost against zero PV and zero EV is unusual: either it reflects legitimate early mobilization or long-lead procurement cost incurred ahead of the building's baseline start (which should ideally have its own small PV allowance if planned), or it is miscoded cost that belongs to a different building or cost code and is inflating the programme's actual cost without any corresponding earned value, which would understate CPI programme-wide.
reasoning: Portfolio-level EVM is a straightforward sum of each component's PV, EV and AC, with the indices recalculated from the totals. Beyond the arithmetic, a competent controls professional should also scan for individual data points that don't fit the expected pattern, such as actual cost being incurred against work with zero planned or earned value, since this is either a legitimate but unplanned early-mobilization cost that should be reflected in the baseline, or a coding error that will distort every rolled-up figure until corrected.
commonMistakes: Averaging the five buildings' CPI/SPI values instead of summing PV/EV/AC and recalculating from the totals.
Not noticing or investigating the Building 5 anomaly (AC without any PV or EV).
Assuming all actual cost must correspond to earned progress without checking for coding errors.
redFlags: Reports the programme CPI/SPI without noticing or flagging the Building 5 data anomaly.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If the $80,000 turns out to be legitimate early procurement cost for Building 5's long-lead structural steel, should the baseline PV be adjusted to reflect it?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests understanding of when a baseline should versus should not be adjusted mid-project for a legitimate but unplanned cost.

skill: Recognizing that risk contingency being drawn down faster than physical progress, with no linkage to logged risk events, signals it is masking routine cost overrun rather than funding genuine risk realization
scenario: A desalination plant project has $1,200,000 of risk contingency allocated within specific control accounts as part of the approved Performance Measurement Baseline (distinct from unallocated Management Reserve). At month 6 of an 18-month programme, $850,000 (71%) of that allocated contingency has already been drawn down, while only 35% of the project's overall BAC has been earned. No specific risk register item has been formally closed out or linked to the drawdown; the project controls team notes it has simply been 'absorbed' into routine monthly cost overruns.
question: Is this a legitimate pattern of contingency usage? What should the project controls team investigate and recommend, and does this change BAC or EAC?
expectedAnswer: This is not a healthy pattern: contingency drawn down at 71% while the project is only 35% complete, with no specific risk event logged against it, strongly suggests the contingency is being used as an unstructured buffer to absorb routine cost overruns rather than to fund genuine, identified risk realization. The team should investigate what specific cost items the $850,000 has actually been charged against, and whether those costs would otherwise have shown up as straightforward unfavorable cost variance in the base estimate if contingency had not been available to absorb them, effectively masking the base CPI. BAC does not change, since this allocated contingency was already part of the approved Performance Measurement Baseline, but EAC should be revised to reflect that with only 29% of contingency remaining and 65% of the project still to execute, the remaining contingency cushion is very likely to be exhausted well before completion, which is a real forecast risk that needs to be reported.
strongAnswer: Adds that going forward, contingency draws should require linkage to a specific, logged risk register item with a documented basis, not be applied as a general cost offset, so that the true underlying cost performance (with contingency stripped out) is visible in CPI, and recommends the report separately show CPI including and excluding contingency draws so leadership can see the base cost trend that the contingency has been masking.
expertAnswer: Recognizes this as a governance and reporting-integrity issue, not just a numbers issue: unlinked, undocumented contingency drawdown at this rate should be escalated as a red flag in its own right, since it indicates either weak cost control discipline (routine overruns being absorbed without proper variance reporting) or, in the worst case, a deliberate attempt to keep the base CPI looking healthier than it actually is by hiding overruns inside the contingency line; recommends an immediate, itemized reconciliation of the $850,000 against specific cost transactions, and treating any further undocumented drawdown as a control-account level variance requiring its own explanation, exactly as if it were unfavorable AC.
explanation: Contingency drawn down far faster than physical progress, with no linkage to specific realized risk events, is a strong indicator it is masking routine cost overrun rather than funding genuine risk. BAC remains unchanged since the contingency was already part of the approved baseline, but EAC should be revised upward to reflect that the remaining contingency cushion will very likely be exhausted before project completion, and the practice of undocumented drawdown should be tightened going forward.
reasoning: This tests whether the candidate understands contingency as a specific, risk-linked budget reserve rather than a general-purpose cushion, and can recognize when its usage pattern (rate of drawdown relative to progress, absence of risk-event linkage) itself becomes diagnostic evidence of an underlying cost problem being hidden rather than managed. A senior controls professional should treat unexplained contingency consumption with the same scrutiny as an unfavorable cost variance, because in substance it often is one.
commonMistakes: Treating contingency drawdown as a routine, unremarkable line item as long as the total project remains within overall budget.
Not comparing the rate of contingency consumption against the rate of physical progress.
Confusing this allocated, PMB-level contingency with unallocated Management Reserve, and concluding BAC should change when it should not.
redFlags: Would not flag 71% contingency consumption at 35% physical progress as a concern requiring investigation.
Cannot explain why undocumented contingency drawdown can mask a true cost problem in the base CPI.
p6Checks: Reconcile the $850,000 drawdown against specific cost transactions and control accounts to identify what it actually paid for.
Check whether CPI, calculated with contingency-funded costs excluded from AC, shows a materially different (likely worse) trend than the reported blended CPI.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If the itemized reconciliation shows the $850,000 was genuinely spent on a documented, unforeseen ground condition, does your recommendation change?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate's conclusion is evidence-based rather than an automatic assumption of misuse.

skill: Calculating a favorable VAC forecast and cautioning against over-relying on it when SPI is unfavorable
scenario: A combined-cycle power plant package has BAC = $60,000,000. At the data date, PV = $26,000,000, EV = $24,500,000, and AC = $23,000,000, so the package is showing favorable cost performance but is slightly behind on planned work volume.
question: Calculate CPI, SPI, EAC (typical-variance formula) and VAC. Should the project team treat the forecast underrun (positive VAC) as a reliable, bankable result given the unfavorable SPI? What would you caution leadership about?
explanation: CPI = EV/AC = 24,500,000/23,000,000 = 1.065. SPI = EV/PV = 24,500,000/26,000,000 = 0.942. EAC = BAC/CPI = 60,000,000/1.065 = approximately $56,338,000. VAC = BAC - EAC = 60,000,000 - 56,338,000 = approximately $3,662,000 (favorable, a forecast underrun). While the underrun is real based on current data, it should not be treated as a locked-in, bankable result: the CPI-based EAC assumes current cost efficiency (1.065) continues for all remaining work, but the project is also behind schedule (SPI 0.942), and schedule slippage commonly creates downstream cost pressure, extended site overheads, possible liquidated-damages exposure, or a need to accelerate remaining work, that a purely cost-index-driven EAC does not capture. Leadership should be cautioned that the favorable VAC is a snapshot forecast conditional on cost efficiency holding and on the schedule slippage not translating into additional cost, not a guaranteed final outcome.
reasoning: This tests whether the candidate can calculate a full EVM index/forecast set correctly and also apply appropriate professional caution to a favorable forecast that coexists with an unfavorable secondary signal (SPI). A VAC calculated purely from CPI, while numerically correct as a snapshot, does not account for cost risk that an unfavorable schedule position commonly introduces later in a project, and reporting VAC without that caveat risks setting an expectation that may not hold.
commonMistakes: Reporting the favorable VAC to leadership as a confirmed underrun without qualifying it against the unfavorable SPI.
Calculating VAC as EAC - BAC instead of BAC - EAC, inverting the sign.
Assuming a favorable CPI-based EAC already accounts for schedule-driven cost risk.
redFlags: Presents the $3.66 million forecast underrun as a firm, bankable result without any qualification about schedule risk.
p6Checks: Check the CPM forecast finish date against baseline to quantify how far behind the project actually is in time, beyond what SPI alone conveys.
Review whether any extended-duration cost items (site overheads, equipment rental) are contractually tied to the finish date and would be affected if the schedule slippage persists or worsens.

followUpQuestions.prompt: What specific evidence would make you more confident the favorable VAC will actually be realized rather than eroded by schedule-driven cost pressure?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests ability to identify concrete corroborating evidence (e.g., a validated recovery plan, confirmed absence of extended-duration cost exposure) rather than accepting or rejecting the forecast on instinct.

subcategory: Data Quality Prerequisites for EVM Reporting
skill: Identifying what critical information is missing before accepting a bare CPI/SPI = 1.00 report at face value
scenario: A correctional facility expansion project's monthly cost report to the client consists of a single line: 'CPI = 1.00, SPI = 1.00 - project performing exactly to plan.' No supporting detail, trend history, or control-account breakdown is provided.
question: What critical information is missing before you would trust this report at face value, and why does each item matter?
expectedAnswer: Missing: whether these are cumulative figures (which tend to stabilize toward 1.00 over time even when recent performance has changed) or current-period figures, since a cumulative 1.00 can mask a recent unfavorable trend; whether the figures are broken down by control account/package, since a project-wide 1.00 can result from offsetting favorable and unfavorable packages that individually need attention; whether Actual Cost includes proper accruals for work performed but not yet invoiced, since omitting accruals can produce an artificially favorable (or exactly-1.00-looking) CPI; whether progress (EV) is based on an objective, verified rules-of-credit system or on self-reported, unverified percent-complete estimates, since the latter is easily manipulated toward a comfortable-looking number; and a trend view over the last several periods, since a single data point cannot show whether 1.00 is a stable result or a coincidental crossing point in a volatile trend.
strongAnswer: Adds that it is also worth checking whether the PV baseline itself remains valid and unmanipulated (has it been quietly re-baselined to make the actuals look better), and whether any known risks or pending change orders exist that could move these figures materially in the near term, since a snapshot of exactly 1.00 with no forward-looking context gives false confidence about stability.
expertAnswer: Notes that an unqualified 'CPI = 1.00, SPI = 1.00' report with no supporting detail should itself be treated as a red flag about the maturity of the reporting process, not just the project's performance, since a credible EVM report always shows trend, breakdown, and basis of measurement; recommends the project controls function establish a minimum reporting standard, cumulative and current-period trend, control-account breakdown, accrual basis stated, rules-of-credit basis stated, that any report must meet before being accepted as a basis for client or management decision-making, rather than accepting a bare summary number at face value regardless of how favorable it looks.
explanation: A bare 'CPI = 1.00, SPI = 1.00' figure, without trend history, control-account breakdown, stated accrual basis, and stated progress-measurement basis, cannot be trusted at face value: each of these missing items could individually explain an apparently perfect but misleading result, from cumulative smoothing to offsetting variances to omitted accruals to unverified self-reported progress.
reasoning: This tests the candidate's instinct to interrogate a suspiciously clean, headline EVM result rather than accept it uncritically, precisely because CPI and SPI both equal to exactly 1.00 with zero supporting detail is, in real project controls practice, more often a sign of an underdeveloped or oversimplified report than a genuine, verified finding, and a competent controls professional should know exactly which supporting data points would confirm or disprove it.
commonMistakes: Accepting 'CPI = 1.00, SPI = 1.00' as self-evidently good news without asking for supporting detail.
Not distinguishing cumulative from current-period figures when interpreting an EVM index.
Not considering that offsetting variances across control accounts can produce a misleadingly tidy project-wide figure.
redFlags: Treats a bare, unsupported CPI/SPI = 1.00 report as trustworthy without requesting any further detail.

followUpQuestions.prompt: If you request the control-account breakdown and find one package at CPI 1.40 and another at CPI 0.70 exactly offsetting to a project-wide 1.00, what would you recommend reporting instead?
followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests ability to move from diagnosis to a concrete, more informative reporting recommendation.

skill: Quantifying how a large Level-of-Effort budget share mechanically dilutes a blended SPI and masks genuine schedule slippage in discrete field work
scenario: An EPC project has BAC = $40,000,000, split between home office project management/engineering support, budgeted at $14,000,000 (35% of BAC) and earned using Level of Effort (LOE, meaning EV is credited automatically in lockstep with PV regardless of actual output, so LOE's own SPI is always exactly 1.0 by definition), and discrete field construction activities, budgeted at $26,000,000 (65% of BAC) and earned using objective, verifiable progress measurement. At the data date, PV for the LOE scope is $7,000,000 (EV = $7,000,000, by definition). PV for the field scope is $13,000,000, but EV for the field scope is only $9,750,000, a true field SPI of 0.75, genuinely behind.
question: Calculate the blended project-wide SPI. Then calculate the true field-only SPI. Explain why the blended figure understates how far behind the project's discrete, deliverable-based work actually is, and what you would recommend reporting instead.
expectedAnswer: Blended PV = 7,000,000 + 13,000,000 = $20,000,000. Blended EV = 7,000,000 + 9,750,000 = $16,750,000. Blended SPI = 16,750,000/20,000,000 = 0.8375. Field-only SPI = EV(field)/PV(field) = 9,750,000/13,000,000 = 0.75. The blended SPI (0.8375) looks materially healthier than the true field SPI (0.75) purely because the LOE scope, 35% of total BAC, mechanically always earns exactly 100% of its planned value every period by definition, contributing no genuine schedule signal but diluting the blended figure upward. Since LOE has no discrete deliverable, its SPI can never reveal a schedule problem, so blending it with genuinely measurable field work systematically understates how far behind the deliverable-producing scope actually is. The recommendation is to report SPI separately for LOE-earned scope and for discrete, objectively-measured scope, and to treat only the discrete-scope SPI as a genuine schedule health indicator, since the LOE component should be reported (or excluded) as a budget-consumption metric rather than a schedule-performance one.
strongAnswer: Adds that this distortion grows larger, not smaller, as the LOE budget share increases, so projects with very large indirect/support cost bases (a common feature of complex EPC and infrastructure programmes) are structurally more prone to this masking effect than projects with a small LOE share, making the separate-reporting recommendation more, not less, important on exactly the projects where it is most often skipped.
expertAnswer: Recommends this be built into the project's standard EVM reporting template from project set-up, not discovered ad hoc, specifically flagging any project where LOE-earned budget exceeds roughly 15-20% of total BAC as requiring a mandatory LOE-excluded SPI to be shown alongside the blended figure; also notes that because LOE cost itself is real (staff still need to be paid regardless of field progress), a slipping field schedule with a large LOE base compounds cost risk, since home office support costs continue to accrue at the planned (LOE) rate for longer than planned if field completion slips, an indirect cost-growth consequence of schedule slippage that a purely field-focused view would also miss.
explanation: The blended SPI (0.8375) is materially more favorable than the true field-only SPI (0.75) because Level of Effort scope, by definition, always earns exactly its planned value and therefore contributes no genuine schedule signal while diluting the blended average. A competent controls professional should report discrete/measurable-scope SPI separately from LOE-scope SPI, since only the former is a genuine indicator of schedule performance, and should recognize this masking effect grows with the size of the LOE budget share.
reasoning: This tests a genuinely advanced EVM literacy point: SPI's mathematical construction assumes EV meaningfully reflects physical progress, an assumption that Level of Effort earning, by design, violates, since LOE credits value on the passage of time/budget consumption rather than on any verifiable output. Blending LOE and discrete-scope EV together in one project-wide SPI is technically correct arithmetic but analytically misleading, and recognizing this, and correcting for it in reporting, distinguishes an expert-level controls professional from one who calculates indices correctly but does not understand their limitations.
commonMistakes: Reporting only the blended SPI without separating LOE from discrete/measurable scope.
Not recognizing that LOE's SPI is definitionally always 1.0 and therefore contributes zero genuine schedule information.
Assuming a project with a large indirect/support cost base is less exposed to this distortion, when in fact it is more exposed.
redFlags: Reports blended SPI without knowing what share of BAC is LOE-earned.
Cannot explain why LOE's SPI is always exactly 1.0 by definition.
p6Checks: Check which activities in the cost-loaded schedule are assigned a Level of Effort percent-complete type versus Physical or Units, and sum their budgeted cost as a share of total BAC.
Verify whether the reporting template already separates LOE-earned SPI from discrete-scope SPI, and if not, flag this as a reporting gap.

followUpQuestions.purpose: Tests whether the candidate applies proportional judgment rather than a blanket rule.
